Q: ROW_NUMBER() returns non-sequential or "jumpy" results when using ORDER BY on non-unique dates A:

Since session_date isn't unique, SQL Server doesn't have a "tie-breaker" to decide which row comes first, leading to unstable sorting.

According to Microsoft SQL Server Documentation, the ORDER BY clause does not guarantee a deterministic result if the sort keys are not unique.

"If the ORDER BY clause is not unique, the order of the rows is non-deterministic." — Microsoft Learn: ROW_NUMBER (Transact-SQL)

If you want to fix this and get a consistent 1, 2, 3... sequence, add a unique column (like application_id or session_id) as a secondary sort key in your OVER clause:

row_number() over (
    partition by user_id 
    order by session_date, application_id  -- Tie-breaker added here
) as row_num

Q: Are there technical reasons not to use undefined custom elements for everything? A:

Every browser vendor (Google since 2016, Apple since 2017 and Mozilla since 2018) processes EVERY <tag-name> (with a dash) as VALID HTMLElement without using JavaScript!

So, for nearly a decade now, Custom Elements come in 2 flavours:

  • UNdefined Custom Elements : <tag-name> hardly blogged about, even AI wrongly calls them unknown elements, they are not! They pass every HTML Validator because they extend from HTMLElement not HTMLUnknownElement like <tagname> (no dash!)

  • Defined Custom Elements : <tag-name> upgraded/defined with JavaScript, what the whole world thinks Custom Elements are, since every Web Components explanation dives straight into the JavaScript code.

UNdefined Custom Elements are great for layout and styling. Just remember to set the CSS display property. That means every DIV or SPAN can be replaced with a meaningful <tag-name>. Yes! you could have done so for nearly a decade now...

Q: Python re search all multiline blocks in text A:

The problem I observer is that (\n.*)* don't match correctly new lines and can be too greedy.

Try this pattern instead:

\(?select.*(\n(?!.*select).*)*[;\)]

Explanation:

\(? - match literally ( zero or one time due to ?

select - match literally select

.* - match arbitrary character zero or more times

(...) - capturing group

\n - match newline character

(?!...) - negative lookahead

.* - match arbitrary character zero or more times

select - match literally select

.* - match arbitrary character zero or more times

[;\)] - character class [...], match any of characters: ; or )

Q: Convert HDF5 (.h5) to spark dataframes A:

Late reply but we implemented it 2025 with
Spark 4 (on Databricks)
Python 3.12

Main ingredients:

h5py
mapInArrow pyArrow Delta Lake on parquet

1. Distribute file paths to executors

Use Spark's built-in binaryFile reader to discover files. Drop the content column immediately — reading the actual bytes in the driver is a memory killer for large HDF5 files. Pass only the path to each executor and open the file there.

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

files_df = (
    spark.read
    .format("binaryFile")
    .option("pathGlobFilter", "*.h5")
    .load("abfss://container@account.dfs.core.windows.net/data/")
    .drop("content")           # <-- key: don't ship bytes to driver
)

2. Define the output schema

mapInArrow requires a fixed output schema upfront.

from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, DoubleType, IntegerType

output_schema = StructType([
    StructField("batch_id",    StringType(),  nullable=False),  # maps to input files / partition
    StructField("signal_name", StringType(),  nullable=False),
    StructField("timestamp",   DoubleType(),  nullable=False),
    StructField("value",       DoubleType(),  nullable=False),
])

3. The file mapper (runs on executor)

import h5py
import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa
from urllib.parse import urlparse

MAX_ROWS_PER_BATCH = 500_000  # tune to your executor memory and width (column count) of output schema

def map_h5_file(path: str) -> pa.Table:
    """Open one HDF5 file by path and return a PyArrow Table."""
    # strip abfss:// or file:// scheme if your storage driver needs a plain path
    local_path = urlparse(path).path

    rows = {"batch_id": [], "signal_name": [], "timestamp": [], "value": []}
    with h5py.File(local_path, "r") as h5:
        for signal_name, dataset in h5["signals"].items():
            data: np.ndarray = dataset[:]           # shape (N,) or (N, channels)
            timestamps: np.ndarray = h5["timestamps"][:]
            rows["batch_id"].extend([path] * len(timestamps))
            rows["signal_name"].extend([signal_name] * len(timestamps))
            rows["timestamp"].extend(timestamps.tolist())
            rows["value"].extend(data.tolist())

    return pa.table(rows)

4. Wire it up with mapInArrow

mapInArrow streams pa.RecordBatch iterators — one iterator per partition (= one file here). Yield batches to control memory.

from collections.abc import Iterable
import pyarrow as pa

def process_batches(
    batches: Iterable[pa.RecordBatch],
) -> Iterable[pa.RecordBatch]:
    for batch in batches:
        for row in batch.to_pylist():
            table = map_h5_file(row["path"])
            yield from table.to_batches(MAX_ROWS_PER_BATCH)

result_df = files_df.mapInArrow(process_batches, schema=output_schema)

Hint: If you have shared lookup data broadcast it before the mapInArrow call

5. Write to Delta — partition by input batch

Partition by the column that maps to your input file / job batch. This turns future overwrites into single-partition replacements with zero table scan (Delta's replaceWhere).

(
    result_df
    .withColumn("batch_id", result_df["batch_id"])   # already present
    .write
    .format("delta")
    .mode("overwrite")
    .option("mergeSchema", "true")
    .option("replaceWhere", "batch_id = 'my-run-id'")   # atomic replace of one partition
    .partitionBy("batch_id")
    .saveAsTable("my_catalog.my_schema.signals")
)

Full call stack

ingest()
 ├── spark.read(binaryFile).drop("content")   # driver: distribute paths
 ├── .repartition(file_count)                 # 1 file = 1 partition
 ├── .mapInArrow(process_batches, schema)     # executor: open h5 by path
 │       └── map_h5_file(path)               #           h5py reads locally
 │               └── yield pa.RecordBatch    #           stream back in chunks
 └── .write.format("delta")
         .partitionBy("batch_id")            # overwrite one partition, not the table
         .saveAsTable(...)

Additional hints:

  • be aware of memory consumption. hdf5 is compressed, small files may be large. spark tends to coalesce multiple small files into one partition. prevent with repartition(file_count)
  • dropping content is only important for big and many files, executors need access to the folder
  • for big files you can tune memory further by not yielding content of one file at once but looping through hdf5 content and yielding parts, this of course implies multiple reads of every file
